<common-name datatype="string">3-keto-L-gulonate-6-phosphate decarboxylase UlaD</common-name>

<comment datatype="string">3-keto-L-gulonate 6-phosphate decarboxylase is an enzyme in the pathway of anaerobic L-ascorbate degradation.
<p>
Crystal structures of the UlaD protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11900527">Wise02</a>], UlaD complexed with substrate, reaction intermediate and product analogs [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14567674">Wise03</a>], and several mutants [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15157078">Wise04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15697207">Wise05</a>] have been determined.  The enzyme is as a dimer of antiparallel (&beta;/&alpha;)<sub>8</sub> barrels in the crystal structure [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11900527">Wise02</a>].  Active site residues and catalytic mechanisms involving a Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion-stabilized <i>cis</i>-1,2-enediolate intermediate have been studied [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11900527">Wise02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14567674">Wise03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15157077">Yew04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15157078">Wise04</a>].  
<p>
Kinetic properties of active site mutants have been analyzed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15157077">Yew04</a>].  Certain changes to active site residues can enhance the D-<i>arabino</i>-hex-3-ulose 6-phosphate synthase (HPS) activity of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15697206">Yew05</a>].  The structural basis of the effect on the catalytic properties of the enzyme has been explored [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15697207">Wise05</a>].
<p>
UlaD: "<b>u</b>tilization of <b>L</b>-<b>a</b>scorbate" [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11741871">Yew02</a>]</comment>

<common-name datatype="string">L-ascorbate specific PTS enzyme II</common-name>

<comment datatype="string">UlaABC, the L-ascorbate PTS permease belongs to the functional superfamily of the phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) -dependent, sugar transporting phosphotransferase system (PTS<sup>sugar</sup>). The PTS<sup>sugar</sup> transports and simultaneously phosphorylates its sugar substrates in a process called group translocation (reviewed in [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8246840">Postma93</a>]. The ascorbate PTS transporter takes up exogenous L-ascorbate, releasing the phosphate ester, L-ascorbate-6-phosphate, into the cell cytoplasm in preparation for metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>]. 
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 can ferment L-ascorbate only when it is supplied at low concentrations (< 20mM) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11741871">Yew02</a>]. Aerobic utilization of L-ascorbate can be observed under specific conditions. The L-ascorbate PTS permease contributes to transport under aerobic conditions along with another unidentified transporter [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17906139">Campos07</a>]. 
<p>
UlaA is a homodimeric integral membrane protein, <i>ulaB</i> encodes a predicted hydrophilic protein containing an Enzyme IIB PTS domain and <i>ulaC</i> contains an Enzyme IIA PTS domain [<a href="/ECOLI/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bREIZERGENOMESCITECH153%5d">Reizer96b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15153772">Hvorup03a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25686089">Luo15</a>]. UlaABC is the only member of the distinct PTS L-ascorbate family of transporters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24225317">Saier14</a>].
<p>
All three components of the L-ascorbate PTS transporter are necessary for the anaerobic uptake of L-ascorbate <I>in vivo</I> and the phosphorylation of L-ascorbate <I>in vitro</I>. The L-ascorbate PTS transporter requires the general PTS enzymes <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PTSI-MONOMER">Enzyme I</a> (PtsI) and <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PTSH-MONOMER">HPr</a> (PtsH) for transport and phosphorylation of its substrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>]. The overall PTS-mediated phosphoryl transfer reaction can be represented as:
<p>
PEP &rarr; Enzyme I-P<sup>his189</sup> &rarr; HPR-P<sup>his15</sup> &rarr; Enzyme IIA-P<sup>his68</sup> &rarr; Enzyme IIB-P<sup>cys9</sup> - (Enzyme IIC) &rarr; L-ascorbate-6-phosphate 
<p>
<i>ulaABC</i> forms an operon with three other genes (<i>ulaDEF</i>) required for the utilisation of L-ascorbate [<a href="/ECOLI/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bREIZERGENOMESCITECH153%5d">Reizer96b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>]. <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=G7854">ulaR</a> acts as the repressor of the <I>ula</I> regulon [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374842">Campos02</a>]. The <I>ula</I> regulon is subject to glucose repression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14996803">Campos04</a>].
<p>
A mutation of UlaA conferred lactoperoxidase tolerance by an unkown mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16209909">De05b</a>].
<p>
<i>ula</i>: utilization of l-ascorbate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11741871">Yew02</a>]
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">UlaABC, the L-ascorbate PTS permease belongs to the functional superfamily of the phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) -dependent, sugar transporting phosphotransferase system (PTS<sup>sugar</sup>). The PTS<sup>sugar</sup> transports and simultaneously phosphorylates its sugar substrates in a process called group translocation (reviewed in [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8246840">Postma93</a>]. The ascorbate PTS transporter takes up exogenous L-ascorbate, releasing the phosphate ester, L-ascorbate-6-phosphate, into the cell cytoplasm in preparation for metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>]. 
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 can ferment L-ascorbate only when it is supplied at low concentrations (< 20mM) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11741871">Yew02</a>]. Aerobic utilization of L-ascorbate can be observed under specific conditions. The L-ascorbate PTS permease contributes to transport under aerobic conditions along with another unidentified transporter [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17906139">Campos07</a>]. 
<p>
UlaA is a homodimeric integral membrane protein, <i>ulaB</i> encodes a predicted hydrophilic protein containing an Enzyme IIB PTS domain and <i>ulaC</i> contains an Enzyme IIA PTS domain [<a href="/ECOLI/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bREIZERGENOMESCITECH153%5d">Reizer96b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15153772">Hvorup03a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25686089">Luo15</a>]. UlaABC is the only member of the distinct PTS L-ascorbate family of transporters [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24225317">Saier14</a>].
<p>
All three components of the L-ascorbate PTS transporter are necessary for the anaerobic uptake of L-ascorbate <I>in vivo</I> and the phosphorylation of L-ascorbate <I>in vitro</I>. The L-ascorbate PTS transporter requires the general PTS enzymes <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PTSI-MONOMER">Enzyme I</a> (PtsI) and <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=PTSH-MONOMER">HPr</a> (PtsH) for transport and phosphorylation of its substrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>]. The overall PTS-mediated phosphoryl transfer reaction can be represented as:
<p>
PEP &rarr; Enzyme I-P<sup>his189</sup> &rarr; HPR-P<sup>his15</sup> &rarr; Enzyme IIA-P<sup>his68</sup> &rarr; Enzyme IIB-P<sup>cys9</sup> - (Enzyme IIC) &rarr; L-ascorbate-6-phosphate 
<p>
<i>ulaABC</i> forms an operon with three other genes (<i>ulaDEF</i>) required for the utilisation of L-ascorbate [<a href="/ECOLI/reference.html?type=CITATION-REFERENCE&object=%5bREIZERGENOMESCITECH153%5d">Reizer96b</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>]. <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=G7854">ulaR</a> acts as the repressor of the <I>ula</I> regulon [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12374842">Campos02</a>]. The <I>ula</I> regulon is subject to glucose repression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12644495">Zhang03h</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14996803">Campos04</a>].
<p>
A mutation of UlaA conferred lactoperoxidase tolerance by an unkown mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16209909">De05b</a>].
<p>
<i>ula</i>: utilization of l-ascorbate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11741871">Yew02</a>]
</comment>
